item.title: JSConf 2009: the community that didn't know it existed
item.description: In April 2009 about 130 people met in a hotel outside Washington for a conference about JavaScript itself. It nearly didn't happen, and its format, its side room and its name spread around the world.
item.content:encoded:
The conference that gave JavaScript developers a community was nearly cancelled for lack of interest, and by the end of its second day it had been promised to another continent.

JSConf 2009 is a conference devoted to the programming language we all love to hate and hate to love, JavaScript.

That is the first sentence of the About page on the JSConf 2009 site, which is still online with its early bird banner intact: $450 if you register by March 11, 2009. The pitch goes on in the same key. "Come to this conference if you love JavaScript, come if you hate it, come if you don't even know how to program." It describes JavaScript as "a language that often gets overlooked." As an advertisement for two days of your time, it is unusually willing to concede the other side's case.

The conference took place on April 24 and 25, 2009, at the Hotel Palomar in Rosslyn, Virginia, which the site's header rounds up to "Washington, DC USA." About 130 people came. Sixteen talks were on the main program, and a side room took whoever else had something to say. Before the year was out there was a JSConf in Berlin, and the name eventually went on events in more than a dozen countries. I'd argue the format of those two days, down to the tours for attendees' partners, is still roughly what a community tech conference looks like.

Ajax had a conference. JavaScript didn't.

It is not that web developers had nowhere to go before 2009. There was The Ajax Experience, with Ajaxian's Ben Galbraith and Dojo's Alex Russell on the bill, first in San Francisco on May 10 to 12, 2006 and then in Boston that October. The libraries had their own gatherings. In September 2007 John Resig announced "the first all-day jQuery mini-conference" for October 27 in Boston, and the next year's announcement reported that "over 100 jQuery developers" had turned up. That second jQuery Camp was scheduled for "the day before The Ajax Experience," which tells you where the centre of gravity was.

So you could attend a conference about a technique, or one about a library. The language underneath them belonged to nobody in particular. Jan Lehnardt, a CouchDB developer who was at the first JSConf, wrote in early May: "Prior to JSConf, there was no conference dedicated to JavaScript developers, heck, even the idea of a JavaScript community was hazy at best." The reason Lehnardt gave was that people wrote JavaScript part-time, "in addition to say, Python, PHP or Ruby."

Kevin Dangoor of Mozilla, writing on the plane home, was more careful about the claim, and I'd go with that version: "It was possibly even the first conference to feature JavaScript as a general scripting language in the same vein as Python or Ruby." Python and Ruby both had conferences run by their own communities. JavaScript ran in every browser and had no meeting of its own, and my best guess at the reason is Lehnardt's: most of the people writing it did not think of it as their language.

A deposit and a sold-out sign

The organizers were Chris Williams and Laura Williams, a married couple. Chris Williams had been to RubyFringe in 2008, a small Ruby conference in Toronto, and came home with an opinion. Lehnardt told the story in a 2015 talk on JSConf's history. Williams had "been to a lot of industry conferences," and having now seen one done right, concluded that a lot of them were not very good. Then Williams asked, over instant messenger, what Lehnardt thought about a JavaScript conference. Lehnardt said it was surely a good idea. The reply: "I'm glad you say this, he says, because I'm organising one."

The site's news page keeps the timeline. The dates and the hotel were announced on January 5, 2009, and registration opened on January 23. The About page promised that the organizers had "no ambition or desire to financially profit from it," and that whatever was not spent on "food, drinks, speakers, and, most importantly, you" would go to charity. The format would be "not barcamp-style and not multi-track style, but somewhere between the two." A speaker announcement in February signed off with "Be here or be static!"

Then the tickets did not sell. In Lehnardt's 2015 telling, a few months in, at three in the morning Berlin time, Williams said they might have to cancel. Lehnardt, trying to cheer up a friend while half asleep, offered: "if JSConf is a success I'll bring it to Europe." Williams remembers it the other way round. The jsconf.com account says "I made a deal with him one night that if we pulled this crazy experiment off, he would have to hold one in Europe." Both agree there was a deal.

A couple of weeks later, the story goes, it was time to tell the venue the event was off and ask for the deposit back, which, in Lehnardt's words, "as it turns out it is backed by their mortgage." So that nobody else would sign up and be let down, Williams changed the website to say sold out, closed ticket sales, and drove to the hotel. Near the end of the 45-minute drive there was an email asking how to get one more ticket. Then another. In total there were enough inquiries to pass break-even, and the Williamses, instead of cancelling, confirmed the conference on the spot.

Williams told a shorter version the following year, in a talk about how the conference got made. Dangoor's notes from it record the lesson: "conference tickets don't sell out until they sell out." People need to feel they are about to miss something. The same notes say Williams put 200 hours into the first JSConf.

Sixteen talks and a side room

The agenda opened on Friday at 9:15 with Francisco Tolmasky of 280 North on Objective-J and Cappuccino, and ended on Saturday afternoon with Peter Higgins on Dojo. In between came, among others, TaffyDB, Appcelerator's desktop apps, CouchDB, a server-side framework called Axiom Stack, XMPP in the browser, Joyent's hosted JavaScript platform, PhoneGap, Stoyan Stefanov of Yahoo on performance, jQuery UI and SproutCore. Resig had the last slot on Friday, listed as "Secret Topic," and used part of it to introduce TestSwarm.

Count the venues for the language in that list: the desktop, the phone, the server, the database. The site's front page promised you would "Write JavaScript for the iPhone, Android, and the Blackberry." Roughly half the program was still about the browser. The other half was about everywhere else, and that half is what the recaps dwell on. Brian LeRoux's PhoneGap talk, by the organizers' account, had a major hand in putting #jsconf on Twitter's trending topics.

The recaps read like people who had not expected to enjoy themselves this much. Stefanov called it "hands down, the best conference I've ever attended," and admitted to changing the slides "on the night before the presentation (and after the first night's party)." Dangoor noted "probably 50% fewer bullet points" than at other tech conferences, which is the kind of praise you can only give in 2009.

The side room turned out to matter as much as the ballroom. The agenda had promised "a side room for lightning talks and hackfests." By April the site was calling it Track B, "our free-form 'unconf' style track," with slots handed out by email, first come first served. Lehnardt reported that "the Track B room was packed both days." Stefanov thought there "wasn't a big difference" between speakers and attendees, "since attendees presented just as good content on the B-track as did the A-track."

One of the Track B talks was Dangoor's. Three months earlier, on January 29, Dangoor had published "What Server Side JavaScript needs", which argued that "JavaScript needs a standard way to include other modules," and started a mailing list called ServerJS. In the side room at JSConf, Dangoor showed what the post-conference write-up calls the group's "biggest milestone to date": one small module, math.js, loaded unchanged into five different server-side JavaScript environments. I don't have that demo file. These are the first two files of the sample code in the Modules/1.0 specification the group published, since superseded by 1.1, which also happens to start with a math.js:

// math.js
exports.add = function() {
    var sum = 0, i = 0, args = arguments, l = args.length;
    while (i < l) {
        sum += args[i++];
    }
    return sum;
};

// increment.js
var add = require('math').add;
exports.increment = function(val) {
    return add(val, 1);
};

The group was renamed CommonJS, and the spec's page lists Node.js among its implementations. require and exports were on show in the side room of a 130-person conference, months before Node.js had its turn on a JSConf stage.

Why it worked

The honest answer includes luck, as the sold-out sign shows. But some of it was structural, and each of these is arguable.

The language had left the browser. Lehnardt's write-up points at "the newly kindled research in speeding up JS runtimes" and at JavaScript having "a life on its own on the server." An Ajax conference was a conference about a browser technique. By 2009 the people doing the most interesting things with JavaScript were running it in places where the word Ajax meant nothing, and they had no event to go to.

Nobody owned it. A jQuery event was jQuery's, and a Dojo event was Dojo's. JavaScript had no company behind it and no foundation, so a conference named after the language was neutral ground. The sponsors page lists Mozilla, Yahoo, Joyent, the agency R/GA and Sun's startup programme. Sponsors' people spoke, but no one company's product was the subject of the event. Dojo, jQuery, SproutCore and Cappuccino shared a single track. My read is that this was the first time many of those people had been in a room where no library was the host.

It was small on purpose. The sponsor pitch offered access to "125 of the best and brightest developers in the world," and Dangoor reported the Palomar's rooms "filled almost to overflowing." With one main track and 130 people, by Lehnardt's account "most people met everyone else."

Hospitality was treated as content. Mozilla's sponsorship went to the food. Friday night was an open bar at the top of Union Station, courtesy of R/GA, and Saturday night was Joyent and Sun's. And there was a "significant other track": the April announcement said "Bring your significant others, we will be planning a track just for them" to see Washington while the conference was on. Laura Williams took spouses, partners and families touring Washington while the conference ran, so the evening events were, as Lehnardt put it, "nicely mixed." Lehnardt added a note to the rest of the industry: "Other conference organizers: DO TAKE NOTICE!"

The talks were given away. Every session was filmed, and the videos went up free on the conference site over the following months, one news item at a time. A conference of 130 could not have defined anything by itself. The recordings and a week of blog posts titled things like "the best conference you couldn't attend" did the rest.

The money was somebody's house. This is the force that is easy to leave out. A year later Williams wrote "Hug a Conference Organizer", which lays out the arithmetic: "roughly 55% of your budget" goes to the venue, a two-day event for 150 people needs "about $50,000" just to secure speakers, food and drink, and break-even without sponsors is "$189 per day per person." The organizer personally guarantees the hotel's room block. A community conference with no company behind it existed because two people were willing to carry that risk.

A franchise with two rules

At the closing announcements on day two, Williams asked Lehnardt to stand, repeated the three-in-the-morning promise to the room, and told the audience that if they thought the conference had been a success, they should let Jan know. Lehnardt's speaker notes record the reaction in a single word, which I'll leave on Speaker Deck.

Lehnardt had, the day before, met Holger Blank and Malte Ubl at the bar. The three of them ran JSConf EU in Berlin on November 7 and 8, 2009. The JSConf 2009 site announced it in August with a line Lehnardt was still repeating six years later: the first conference "proved to be the homecoming of a JavaScript community that didn't know it existed." In Berlin, Ryan Dahl presented a project called Node.js. Ubl's post with the video says "Ryan received standing ovations for his talk and he really deserved it!" That talk is its own story.

The second American JSConf, in April 2010, was pirate themed, "for reasons I still have never asked about," as Charlie Robbins said in a 2015 talk. Its schedule shows what the first year had taught. Track B is now a full column beside Track A, every slot reading "Open Slot. Register Now!" Douglas Crockford opened. Brendan Eich was smuggled in as a surprise. Ted Leung, attending for the first time, wrote that "the conference reminds me of PyCon in its early days," and that it had been put on by "a 10 person staff."

How the name spread is written down on jsconf.com. JSConf calls itself "a very loose federation of developers who share the same general idea about how a technical conference should be held." There are two rules for using the name. "You must have attended an existing JSConf event," and "You must have an existing JSConf organizer as oversight." Each event is run and financed locally. The overseer's main job, the page says, is to be the person outside the planning who can say "It will work out, don't worry," which is the job Lehnardt did in 2009. The same page tells most people not to bother: "most times it is better to run a 'JSConf like' event with a different name."

Plenty did both. The jsconf.com front page lists JSConf events from Budapest to Bengaluru, and a longer "family" that includes NodeConf, CascadiaJS and Web Rebels. By Lehnardt's 2015 count, more than 50 events with "well over 50000 attendees" traced their origin to that ballroom.

Chris and Laura Williams stepped back in 2015, after a farewell event that December called JSConf US Last Call. Its About page explains that after a serious illness in the family, JSConf US "will be on hold for the foreseeable future." JSConf EU called its 2019 event, "our 10th anniversary," the last edition "in its current form." The name outlived both. JSConf US did come back under that name; its 2019 site advertises Carlsbad, California that August. And in October 2025 JSConf North America was held in Maryland, "back under the OpenJS Foundation."

What it left behind

An identity, which is odder than it sounds. Lehnardt described the mood changing after lunch on the first day: "We are slowly starting to realise that we are JavaScript people who do Ruby on the side, Python on the side and PHP on the side." On that account, before 2009 "JavaScript developer" was mostly something a Rails or PHP developer also was. I can't measure that, but I'd argue the job title you see everywhere now needed a room in which people could try it on, and that the conference did less to serve a community than to convince one it existed.

The module system had its outing on the unscheduled track. Every require() in a Node codebase follows the CommonJS convention that was demonstrated in the side room in April 2009, months before Dahl's talk in Berlin. The work was done on a mailing list. The conference's part was to give it an audience, and it did that in the room nobody had curated. JSConf did not invent the open slot. Its own agenda credits the "-camp" style, and Lehnardt's verdict on Track B was "BarCamps rule." What it showed is why a curated conference should keep one: that is where things turn up that a program committee would not have picked, because in April nobody knew they mattered.

The name was governed like open source. The two rules are a fork policy. Anyone can copy the format, and the site encourages it, but the name is protected so that it keeps meaning something. By 2010 the conference's own site was writing it as "JSConf™." Open-source projects handle code and trademarks the same way. It fits that the North American event is now run under the OpenJS Foundation, whose project list includes Node.js. The conference and the runtime its European sibling introduced ended up under one roof.

Its code of conduct was forked too. The 2012 JSConf site carries a code of conduct with a paragraph that starts "JSConf is dedicated to providing a harassment-free conference experience for everyone," followed by a list of who everyone includes. The 2019 site claims JSConf "was one of the first conferences to implement and enforce" one. I can't rank who was first. I can say the text travelled: the page for React.js Conf in January 2015 says its code of conduct "is borrowed from JSConf Code of Conduct." The boilerplate at the bottom of a conference site today was once a decision an organizer had to make.

The fix became the next problem. The "sold out" notice saved the first JSConf, and the lesson Williams drew from it was that people sign up when they fear missing out. Robbins noted in 2015 that JSConf in 2010 "sold out, albeit a bit slower than it does today." Scarcity is what made the event feel like something. I'd argue it is also what made the better-known community conferences hard to get into for anyone not already on the inside. The later JSConf sites show the organizers pushing the other way: the 2019 one advertises scholarships, and the Last Call one a call for speakers "designed to spotlight the new faces and ideas in the community." My reading is that they were working against an effect their own first lesson had created.

The takeaway

The first JSConf was sixteen talks and a side room in a hotel across the river from Washington, attended by about 130 people, paid for at the organizers' personal risk, and saved by a "sold out" notice that was not yet true. What it produced was mostly social. People who used JavaScript on the side of some other job spent two days together and left describing themselves differently. The module convention, the European sequel and the stage Node.js was launched from all followed from that.

Its lasting invention was a way of running the thing: small, single-track with an open room beside it, generous to the point of feeding people properly and looking after their families, recorded and given away, and passed on to anyone who had attended one and could find an earlier organizer to tell them it would work out. Robbins put the principle on a slide in 2015 as "PEOPLE >>> SOFTWARE." Some of the software shown in that ballroom is still in use and a good deal of it is not. The format has outlasted most of it.

item.title: The webmaster: a mailbox that became a job
item.description: "Webmaster" was coined as a mail alias on a style page, grew into the title for whoever ran the whole site, and faded, while the address in the footer link outlived the job.
item.content:encoded:
For about a decade, a website had one person behind it and one address at the bottom of the page where you could reach them. The address has lasted far longer than the job.

Hi Webmaster!
  ...
Can you help?

Those are the greeting and the question from an email sent on March 16, 1995, under the subject "Error 404". The parts I left out are one sentence of explanation, a sign-off and a pasted error: "WWW Alert: Fatal Error 404 No Match Found for", followed by an address on CERN's server. The World Wide Web Consortium still keeps the message in a folder of its history archive called MailArchive/webmaster.

The folder is worth a visit. Its index covers three weeks, from March 14 to April 4, 1995, and lists 405 messages. That is about nineteen a day, arriving in a mailbox that existed because a style guide had suggested it. The subject lines include "help", "Need help!", "test", "Weather", "healing", "Search Frustrations" and a great many "(no subject)".

The word in that greeting became a job title, a magazine survey category, a line in an RFC, the name of a Google product and, eventually, something people stopped calling themselves. This essay follows the word and the address together, because they started as the same thing. "Webmaster" was a mailbox first and an occupation second.

Before: sign your initials

Email had worked out its own version of the problem years earlier. A mail system needs a human who can be told that the mail system is broken, and the address for that human cannot depend on knowing their name. So the name was fixed in advance. As a later RFC put it, the mail standards require "the presence of a <POSTMASTER@domain> mailbox name on all hosts that have an SMTP server."

The early web had no equivalent, and at first it did not think it needed one. W3C keeps a snapshot of CERN's web pages from November 3, 1992, and in it is a page of etiquette for people publishing on the new system. Its first rule is headed "Sign it!":

Make a page for yourself with your mail address and phone number. At the bottom of files for which you are responsible, put a small note -- say just your initials -- and link it to that page.

The page follows its own advice. Here is its last line, exactly as served:

<ADDRESS><A NAME=0 HREF=http://info.cern.ch./hypertext/TBL_Disclaimer.html>Tim BL</A>

That is the original footer contact link, and it points at a person. In 1992 responsibility on the web was per document. Each page had an author, the author had a phone book entry, and if something was wrong you wrote to whoever's initials were at the bottom. The same page tells you to give your server a root page for outsiders and a stable alias like www.dom.edu. It has no word for the person who runs the server, and no address for them either.

A word coined on a style page

The later version of that page, which W3C still serves with a "1992-95" credit at the bottom, has a new section. It is called "An alias for yourself":

You should make a mail alias "webmaster" on the server machine so that people who have problems with your server can mail you about it easily. This is similar to the "postmaster" alias for people who have mail problems with your machine.

And near the top, Tim Berners-Lee added a note that is rare among etymologies, in that the coiner is standing right there: "As a server administrator, or webmaster as they are known (the term having been coined on this page, below) you should make sure this applies to your data."

When exactly? The November 1992 snapshot does not have the section. The later page carries a remark dated "[3/94]". Merriam-Webster gives the first known use of "webmaster" as 1993. So my best guess is 1993, and I can't narrow it further than "after November 1992".

Look at what was actually defined. It was a mail alias, built by analogy with one that already existed, for "people who have problems with your server". It described who should receive complaints. Nothing in it said the recipient should also write the pages, draw the buttons or choose the colours.

In fact the same page argues against it. In the very next section, "Delegating control", Berners-Lee wrote: "Maybe the server administrator has no responsibility at all for the actual content of the data, in which case he or she should just keep the machine running properly." The person who coined the word separated server from content almost in the same breath. The web then spent a few years ignoring the distinction.

The address gets wired in

The other half of the footer link arrived in December 1994. RFC 1738, the URL specification that Berners-Lee co-edited, defined a mailto scheme "used to designate the Internet mailing address of an individual or service." Note the last two words. With the alias and the scheme together, any page could end with a link in this pattern (the domain here is the etiquette page's own example):

<A HREF="mailto:webmaster@dom.edu">

There was a more formal route too. HTML 3.2, published in January 1997, noted that "REV=made is sometimes used to identify the document author, either the author's email address with a mailto URL, or a link to the author's home page." Lynx did something with it. Its user guide still documents a c command to "send a mail message to the owner of the current document", which works when the page's head contains this:

<LINK REV="made" HREF="mailto:user@somedomain.com">

Then the servers picked the idea up. Apache's sample configuration, in the 1.3 branch, has these lines:

#
# ServerAdmin: Your address, where problems with the server should be
# e-mailed.  This address appears on some server-generated pages, such
# as error documents.
#
ServerAdmin you@your.address

That comment undersells it. The 1.3 source builds the Internal Server Error page from a fixed text with the address dropped into the middle: "Please contact the server administrator, [the address] and inform them of the time the error occurred, and anything you might have done that may have caused the error." So at the moment a site failed worst, the server printed the webmaster's email address and suggested the visitor consider their own part in it.

The last step was ratification. In May 1997 D. Crocker of the Internet Mail Consortium published RFC 2142, "Mailbox Names for Common Services, Roles and Functions". It did not claim to invent anything. "Other protocols have defacto standards for well known mailbox names," it says, "such as <USENET@domain> for NNTP (see [RFC977]), and <WEBMASTER@domain> for HTTP". Its table lists WEBMASTER against HTTP, with WWW as a synonym. It also insists that case must not matter, which produces the best sentence in the document: "POSTMASTER, postmaster, Postmaster, PostMaster, and even PoStMaStEr are to be treated the same".

A few years after a suggestion on a style page, the alias was on the standards track.

How an alias became a job

Meanwhile the name on the mailbox had become the name of the person reading it. An undated Princeton Review career profile of the webmaster cites a 1996 survey by Web Week magazine in which "35 percent of respondents reported their official title as 'Webmaster' (either exclusively or in addition to another title), while none reported having that title the previous year."

Jay Hoffmann, who writes The History of the Web, describes the role as it was understood by then: webmasters "were at once the architect and the builder of a website, responsible for every bit of code and content that came through it." Hoffmann's candidate for the first of them is Louise Addis, a librarian at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, who ran the day-to-day operation of the lab's early website. Why did one title swallow the whole site? I count four forces, and none of them was a mistake.

The sites were small. Hoffmann's description of a mid-1990s business site is a front door to the internet, "updated weekly, maybe even less". One person could keep several of those going.

The stack was shallow. A site was a directory of files, a server with one configuration file, and maybe a folder of CGI scripts. All of it fitted in one head. This is my own reading of the period's software, but the Apache file above is a fair exhibit: one setting for who gets told about problems, and it takes a single address.

The institutions were used to it. The web grew up in labs and universities. As Hoffmann puts it, these were places where "it was not uncommon for people to have these pet projects on top of their existing work". A librarian who also ran a web server was normal there.

Nobody knew what else to call it. Organizations wanted a website before they had any idea which department a website belonged to. A webmaster, in Hoffmann's words, "was brought in by a business or a client or an organization when they needed a website and they didn't know who else to call." Hiring one person with a new title was easier than deciding whether the thing was IT, marketing or publishing.

What the mailbox actually got

The alias was meant for "people who have problems with your server". The W3C archive shows what arrived instead, and it is the best job description of a webmaster I have found.

Some of it was exactly what the alias was for. The first message in the archive, from a university in Berlin, is a precise bug report. A geographical listing on W3C's server had grown to 1,118,838 bytes, and the connection gave out after nine minutes: "By that time, we have received the African, Asian and Australian sections and the rest of the world is cut off."

Much of it was not about the server at all. One writer was "desperately looking for a design guide for html documents." One, under the subject "Where I am in here", wrote: "I'm trying to figure out how to get into this network and not having much luck." One message, apart from a name and a signature block, says only: "Hello ! Greetings from Warsaw", from "a WWW user". To a newcomer, the webmaster of the web's home site was the front desk of the entire internet.

Software authors noticed the pattern. Apache's documentation for ServerAdmin still advises: "It may be worth setting up a dedicated address for this", and gives the reason with some feeling: "users do not always mention that they are talking about the server!"

Then came the mail nobody had asked for. RFC 2142 had seen it coming. Its entire security section is one sentence: "Denial of service attacks (flooding a mailbox with junk) will be easier after this document becomes a standard, since more systems will support the same set of mailbox names." An address that everyone can guess, printed in a link that any program can read, is a gift to anyone compiling a mailing list.

Webmasters coped in two ways. The first was to stop printing the address and let a script build it in the browser, on the theory that a harvesting program reads HTML and does not run JavaScript. This is a typical version, written to run as shown and not taken from any one site:

<script type="text/javascript">
var u = "webmaster";
var h = "example" + ".com";
document.write('<a href="mai' +
  'lto:' + u + '@' + h + '">' +
  u + '@' + h + '<\/a>');
</script>

Wikipedia's article on address munging records the trick and its limit: newer harvesting programs can often run the script themselves.

The second was to replace the link with a form. The standard tool was FormMail, a Perl script from Matt's Script Archive that turned any HTML form into an email. Its page calls it "quite possibily the most used CGI program on the internet, having been downloaded over 2,000,000 times since 1997." View the source of that page and you find a notice, now commented out, dated April 19, 2002: "Several important spam-related security holes have been fixed". The script installed to keep the webmaster out of spammers' lists had spam problems of its own.

Why the title wore out

Hoffmann gives two reasons the role faded, and I think both are right. First, in Hoffmann's words: "Things got too hard for one person to manage." Ambitious sites were now built by teams of art directors, editors, developers and writers, and Hoffmann says of one such site, Word magazine, that it was "well beyond the scope of what one person could reasonably accomplish on their own." Second, things got too easy: visual editors, content management systems and hosted services each took over one of the webmaster's chores, until, in Hoffmann's phrase, "one by one the jobs of the webmaster were peeled away and outsourced to some tool."

The title hung on for a long time at Google. Jens Oliver Meiert writes that on joining Google in 2008, "I joined the 'Webmaster Team,' and we were on Google's webmaster job ladder." The product for site owners was called Google Webmaster Tools until a post on May 20, 2015 announced that it would become Search Console. The announcement was polite about it: "It turns out that the traditional idea of the 'webmaster' reflects only some of you." The users, Google had found, were "hobbyists, small business owners, SEO experts, marketers, programmers, designers, app developers, and, of course, webmasters as well."

Five years later the courtesy was dropped. On November 11, 2020, Google Webmasters Central became Google Search Central, and the post said plainly that "the term is becoming archaic". A user study had shown that "very few web professionals identify themselves as webmasters anymore." The Princeton Review profile had allowed for it. Its outlook for the career warned that "what it means to be a Webmaster today may completely change over the next few years and may even become obsolete."

What the webmaster left behind

The address became a key. This is the part I did not expect. When a certificate authority issues a TLS certificate, it has to check that the applicant controls the domain. The CA/Browser Forum's Baseline Requirements list the permitted methods, and one of them, section 3.2.2.4.4, is to send a random value by email to an address made from "'admin', 'administrator', 'webmaster', 'hostmaster', or 'postmaster'" at the domain and wait for a reply. Whoever reads webmaster@ can be treated as the owner of the site.

That has gone wrong in the way you would predict. In March 2015 Microsoft disclosed an improperly issued certificate for the domain live.fi: "An email account was able to be registered for the live.fi domain using a privileged username, which was subsequently used to request an unauthorized certificate for that domain." The advisory does not say which username it was. Whichever it was, a list of mailbox names that began as a courtesy to people with problems had become a list of credentials. The same document now gives it an end date: the method "SHOULD NOT" be used from March 15, 2026, and from March 15, 2028 a certificate authority "MUST NOT rely on this method".

Every specialty rebuilt the mailbox. When the job split, each piece needed its own way to be reached. RFC 9116, from April 2022, defines security.txt, a file at a well-known path that says who to contact about a vulnerability. It cites RFC 2142, which also reserved a SECURITY@domain mailbox, and its complaint about that convention is that it "provides only a single, email-based channel of communication per domain". It even inherits the old worry, in a section headed "Spam and Spurious Reports". I'd argue security.txt is the 1993 alias, rebuilt for one of the webmaster's descendants.

The defaults still assume one person. Apache's sample virtual host in the current development tree still reads ServerAdmin webmaster@dummy-host.example.com, and the error text still asks you to contact "the server administrator" and describe "the actions you performed just before this error." The software still imagines a single reachable human who owns the machine. Production sites replaced that human with an on-call rotation, which is my comparison and not Apache's, and the visitor's half of the link disappeared in the trade.

The generalist keeps coming back. Meiert's post, written in 2026, argues that AI tools are "allowing a single person to once again manage the entire stack", and that the webmaster may be "leveling up" instead of dead. That is a forecast, and I'd treat it as one. But notice which half of the old role the argument revives. It is the breadth: one person across design, code and servers. The 1993 definition was the other half, the person who answers for the site. Meiert's piece does get to it: "the webmaster orchestrates and takes the responsibility".

The takeaway

The webmaster was an address before it was a job. Berners-Lee's page asked for a mailbox so that a stranger with a problem could reach someone responsible, and it said in the next section that this someone need not be the person who wrote the content. For a few years the sites were small enough that it was the same person anyway, and the industry mistook a coincidence of scale for a profession. When the sites grew, the profession came apart along the line the style page had already drawn.

The breadth went to "full-stack" and now, perhaps, to one person with good tools. The work went to teams. What mostly did not survive is the footer link's promise: that a visitor who found something broken could tell a human, in one click, and that the human could fix it. The address itself is still honoured by mail systems, sample configs and, until 2028, certificate authorities. It is the most durable thing the webmaster built, and on most sites nobody is reading it.

item.title: The IE6 funeral: campaigning to kill a browser
item.description: In March 2010 a Denver web shop buried Internet Explorer 6 in a pine coffin and Microsoft sent flowers. The browser had a fifth of the market that night, and what finally ended it was not persuasion.
item.content:encoded:
In March 2010 a web design shop in Denver held a funeral for a browser that about a fifth of the web was still using, and the company that made the browser sent flowers.

Thanks for the good times, IE6. See you all @ MIX, where we'll show a little piece of IE heaven.

The Internet Explorer Team @ Microsoft

That is the card that came with the arrangement, as TechCrunch printed it the next day. The funeral was on Thursday, March 4, 2010. The hosts were Aten Design Group, and Denver's Westword counted "around a hundred people" in a venue called Forest Room 5. The deceased lay in a pine coffin: stuffed clothes, with a monitor and an IE6 logo where the head should be. Jon Clark of Aten told Computerworld, "I spent a lot of time in the garage making the pine coffin." Many guests wore black. Candles were lit, and several people gave eulogies.

The obituary on ie6funeral.com, quoted by Computerworld a week earlier, gave the cause:

Internet Explorer Six, resident of the interwebs for over 8 years, died the morning of March 1, 2010, in Mountain View, California, as a result of a workplace injury sustained at the headquarters of Google, Inc.

It was survived, the notice went on, by "son Internet Explorer Seven, and grand-daughter Internet Explorer Eight." It was also, by the same article's numbers, running on about 20% of the browsers in use the month before. The funeral was a good joke, and it was the high point of a two-year campaign in which web developers tried to talk the public out of a piece of software. What that campaign could and couldn't do is the part worth keeping.

A browser that outlived its war

Internet Explorer 6 debuted in August 2001 and went out with Windows XP. By then the first browser war was over and Microsoft had won it, so there was no hurry about a sequel. Internet Explorer 7 was not released until October 2006. For five years IE6 was the newest version of the browser nearly everybody had, and a great deal got built to fit it, on the public web and behind company firewalls.

By 2008 the picture had changed everywhere except on those machines. Firefox and Safari were real, IE7 was two years old, and the same page now had to work in all of them and in IE6 as well. Justin Toupin, Aten's founder, described the cost to Computerworld in the mildest terms available: "It does involve, toward the end of a project especially, considerable work adjusting things like CSS and JavaScript to make sure they work." Every reader of this collection can supply their own less mild version.

The stubborn part is that in early 2009, more than seven years in, IE6 still had more users than the newest Firefox. NetApplications figures reported by InfoWorld that February gave it 19.21% of the market against 18.3% for Firefox 3.0. You could not simply stop.

2008: the first notices

The first people to stop were the ones whose customers paid them directly. In July 2008, 37signals announced it would phase out IE6 across all its products on August 15. Their notice, as quoted by InfoQ, said: "Supporting IE 6 means slower progress, less progress, and, in some places, no progress." Apple had told .Mac subscribers that June that the new MobileMe web apps needed Safari 3, Internet Explorer 7 or Firefox 2.

Simon Willison's reaction to 37signals caught the nerve of it: "Interesting move considering BaseCamp is used for communicating with (often corporate) clients." Hold on to that word "corporate."

Norway and the conditional comment

The campaign proper began in Norway in February 2009. Finn.no, an online marketplace and one of the largest sites in the country, started showing IE6 visitors a notice. The Register printed it in English:

Heads up: You're using an older version of Internet Explorer. In order to get the most out of our website, you can get a free update of Internet Explorer. If you're using a work computer, you should contact your IT administrator.

Finn.no said about 17% of its 4.2 million users were on IE6. By February 19, The Register was reporting that two of Norway's three largest newspapers had posted similar messages, along with local papers, search engines, ISPs and the Yellow Pages. On February 20, Peter-Paul Koch put a warning on QuirksMode and titled his post "To Hell With Bad Browsers — the sequel", after Jeffrey Zeldman's 2001 A List Apart article that had told designers to stop coddling Netscape 4. Koch was honest about the limits: "we web developers are mainly preaching to the choir, but some body has to start."

The mechanism is the detail I like best. The notices were delivered by a Microsoft feature. Conditional comments had been in Internet Explorer since version 5: an HTML comment with a condition in it, which IE read and every other browser skipped as an ordinary comment. Here is the snippet Scott Hanselman passed along on February 23, 2009, with its style block and most of its paragraph text cut for length:

<!--[if lte IE 6]>
<div id="ie6msg">
<h4>Did you know that your browser is out of date?</h4>
<p>To get the best possible experience using my website I recommend that you upgrade your browser to a newer version. [...] If you’re using a PC at work you should contact your IT-administrator. [...]</p>
[...]
</div>
<![endif]-->

lte IE 6 means "less than or equal to IE 6." No script, no server code, no user-agent sniffing. As Hanselman put it, "There's no server-side requirement at all." Microsoft had built conditional comments so developers could feed its browser special instructions. Developers used them to feed its users one.

Both notices send you to the same person: your IT administrator. The people writing the banners already knew who actually had the decision.

By August 2009 an American site, IE6 No More, was handing out a similar snippet. IT Pro described the group as tech start-ups led by Weebly, and InfoQ counted more than 70 companies showing the message. The same InfoQ piece quotes Zeldman's line for the year: "IE6 is the new Netscape 4."

Digg asks, YouTube bluffs

That summer two big sites tried opposite approaches. Digg asked. Its IE6 visitors, TechCrunch reported in July 2009, were around 5% of traffic but only 1% of diggs, buries and comments, so Digg polled them on why they hadn't upgraded. Eric Lawrence of the IE team (the post is signed only "Eric") summed up the result: "The dominant answer (32%+37%=69%) was that 'I'm not allowed by my IT department, and I don't have permissions to ignore them.'" Given those answers, TechCrunch reported, Digg was not going to run an upgrade banner any time soon. It would mostly have been nagging people who had no say.

YouTube bluffed, and for ten years nobody outside knew it was a bluff. In 2019 Chris Zacharias, who had been a web developer there, published A Conspiracy To Kill IE6. IE6 was about 18% of YouTube's users and the team had been told support was not optional. So, in Zacharias's telling, a few engineers used a permission set called OldTuber, which YouTube's early engineers had created when the company was folded into Google, and which let its holders commit code with "only the most glancing of code reviews," and shipped a banner above the video player for IE6 users only:

We will be phasing out support for your browser soon. Please upgrade to one of these more modern browsers.

There was no date, because there was no plan. "The text was intentionally vague and the timeline left completely undefined," Zacharias writes. TechCrunch spotted the banner on July 14, 2009, and took it at face value, as did everyone else. Inside Google, two lawyers arrived wanting to know, in Zacharias's words, "Why did you have to put Chrome first?" The engineers showed them that the order of the browser links was random. Then the Google Docs team saw the banner and added one of their own, presumably, Zacharias writes, assuming YouTube had done its diligence. After that, at least one YouTube manager assumed the engineers had copied Docs.

Zacharias gives the result as: "Within one month, our YouTube IE6 user base was cut in half and over 10% of global IE6 traffic had dropped off." Those are one participant's numbers a decade on, and I can't check them. But notice whom the banner reached. Digg's poll, self-selected as it was, had just suggested that most of its IE6 users couldn't upgrade. YouTube is where you go at lunch, and at home. My best guess is that the banner mostly moved home machines, and gave a lot of office workers a reason to bother the IT department, which is exactly what its authors say they daydreamed about.

Microsoft's answer

On August 10, 2009, Dean Hachamovitch, who ran the Internet Explorer team, answered the whole movement in a post called Engineering POV: IE6. It is worth reading in full, because it is the other side's case made straight:

The engineering point of view on IE6 starts as an operating systems supplier. Dropping support for IE6 is not an option because we committed to supporting the IE included with Windows for the lifespan of the product. We keep our commitments.

And on the people the banners were aimed at: "The choice to upgrade software on a PC belongs to the person responsible for the PC. Many PCs don't belong to individual enthusiasts, but to organizations." The post ends: "We will also continue to respect their choice, because their browser is their choice."

It is easy to read that as a defense of IE6. I read it as a description of a trap Microsoft had built for itself and was now, quite sincerely, standing in.

Why it would not die

The browser was a part of the operating system. This is Hachamovitch's point, and it is a matter of contract more than taste. IE6 shipped in Windows XP, so it was owed patches for as long as XP was. Microsoft's lifecycle page shows XP's extended support running to April 2014. A browser that in 2009 felt eight years stale had five years of guaranteed life left. Lawrence made the security half of the argument: if Microsoft dropped support, people "would still use it anyway, just without the benefit of security and reliability patches."

The person at the keyboard was not the customer. A banner addresses a user. The decision belonged to an IT department with, in Hachamovitch's words, "tens or hundreds or thousands of PCs" to keep working on budget, and usually with what Lawrence called "one or two legacy webapps that require IE6." Those apps had been written for the browser of 2001 to 2006 when it was the only browser that mattered. Five years of monoculture had been converted into internal software, and internal software does not get rewritten because a classifieds site in Oslo is annoyed.

Much of it was a long way from the banners. By February 2010, Computerworld reported, IE6 was under 10% in the United States and about 50% of browsers in use in China. An English-language notice on a Denver agency's client sites was never going to touch that.

Upgrading took a decision. Every other force rests on this one. Getting from IE6 to IE7 or IE8 was something a person, or a department, had to choose to do. Software that needs a decision gets one eventually, on the decider's schedule.

Coping in the meantime

While the argument ran, the work went on. Conditional comments kept doing their intended job, which was feeding IE6 its own fixes. Agencies started treating the browser as a decision per project: Computerworld reported that Aten "now evaluates IE6 support for its projects on a case-by-case basis."

Google tried an end run. In September 2009 it released Chrome Frame, a plug-in that put Chrome's rendering engine inside Internet Explorer. A site opted in with one line:

<meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="chrome=1">

That is Microsoft's own compatibility header, borrowed to ask for somebody else's browser. It still needed the plug-in installed, which on a locked-down office PC was the original problem again.

Libraries absorbed the rest, quietly and for years. jQuery carried IE6 in every release until version 2.0 in April 2013, and even then kept a 1.x branch "which does run on IE 6/7/8." A lot of developers stopped thinking about IE6 well before they stopped supporting it, because a dependency was doing the thinking.

The winter it turned

What actually set a date was security and Google, in that order. In January 2010 Google disclosed that it and other companies had been attacked, and a hole in Internet Explorer was soon named as the likely way in. On January 15, Germany's federal information security office, the BSI, recommended that people switch to another browser until a patch arrived. The flaw affected versions 6, 7 and 8, so it was not IE6's fault alone, but a government telling citizens to stop using Internet Explorer changed what an IT department could say out loud.

Two weeks later, on January 29, Google's enterprise blog announced that Google Docs and Google Sites would begin phasing out older browsers: "from March 1 key functionality within these products... won't work properly." In February, YouTube's seven-month-old bluff finally got a real date. The new notice read: "On March 13, we are dropping support for your browser."

That is the "workplace injury" in the obituary, and March 1 is the date of death. Aten posted its invitation, expecting the 30 or 40 people who usually came to its office parties, and got more than 700 RSVPs. "This kind of blew up on us," Toupin said.

Microsoft's part was better judged than it needed to be. The flowers came from the IE team. A company PR representative from Boulder came too and took photographs; "They were really curious about the tone of the event," Clark said. And the card was also an advertisement. MIX was Microsoft's web conference, and on March 16, twelve days after the wake, the IE team used it to show the first IE9 platform preview. That was the little piece of heaven.

The maker joins the campaign

After the funeral, Microsoft stopped defending and started campaigning. In May 2010 its Australian division put up a page with a milk carton on it. Computerworld gives the copy: "You wouldn't drink 9-year-old milk," and then, "So why use a 9-year-old browser?"

On March 4, 2011, which was a year to the day after the wake (I have no evidence that was deliberate), Microsoft launched IE6 Countdown, a site that tracked IE6's share by country with a target of under 1%. The Next Web noted the opening figures: about 12% of the world, and 34.5% in China. The site offered banners for webmasters to put on their own pages. The vendor was now distributing the developers' tactic.

On January 3, 2012, Microsoft announced that the United States had gone under 1%. Roger Capriotti, Microsoft's director of IE marketing, wrote, as quoted on a Microsoft developer blog: "IE6 has been the punch line of browser jokes for a while, and we've been as eager as anyone to see it go away." Microsoft celebrated with a cake. The Register, less festive, pointed out that IE6 was still 7.7% of the world and around a quarter of China, and that Norway, where the banners began, had been the first country under 1%, back in May 2010.

Support for Windows XP, and with it the commitment Hachamovitch had described, ended in April 2014. The browser was twelve and a half years old.

What it left behind

The real fix was removing the decision. In December 2011 Microsoft announced that Internet Explorer would start upgrading itself through Windows Update, following, as iTnews put it, "in the footsteps of rivals Google and Mozilla." Then it went further and announced that after January 12, 2016, "only the most current version of Internet Explorer available for a supported operating system will receive technical support and security updates". Set that beside "their browser is their choice" from 2009. The industry's answer to IE6 was to take the choice away, and to call the result "evergreen." You very likely don't know what version of your browser you are running, and that ignorance is the campaign's most durable achievement.

The funeral moved into a config file. If you have a build toolchain, there's a fair chance your project contains the phrase not dead. It is a Browserslist query, and the README defines dead as "browsers without official support or updates for 24 months." In 2009, deciding to stop supporting a browser took a blog post, a banner and a certain amount of courage. Now it is a default that most teams have never read. I think that is progress, but it is worth knowing that the argument was not settled so much as automated.

The complaint outlived the browser. Zeldman's "IE6 is the new Netscape 4" was already the second link in a chain. In 2011 Paul Irish wrote IE[x] is the new IE6, and in 2015 Nolan Lawson wrote Safari is the new IE. Irish's post has the sharpest diagnosis of the lot: "what's far more important than shipping frequency, is the browser half-life." I'd say IE6's real offence was duration more than any one bug. Any browser tied to an operating system's release schedule inherits the same problem, which is why that sentence keeps getting rewritten with a new name in it.

The tool went the way of the target. Conditional comments, which carried the banners and a decade of IE-only stylesheets, were removed in Internet Explorer 10. Microsoft's own page on the change advises: "consider using feature detection." That is the same advice the previous browser war ended on.

The lawyers asked the right question. A banner on one site halved that site's IE6 audience in a month, by its author's account, and once other Google properties followed, Zacharias writes, "Google had given permission to every other site on the web to add their own." The site belonged to a company that had launched its own browser the year before. The engineers randomized the list and meant it. Still, I'd argue the funeral's cheerful story, in which developers and one big friendly website free the web from a browser monoculture, reads a little differently now that most browsers run on that company's engine.

The takeaway

The IE6 funeral is remembered as the day the web's developers buried the browser they hated. What the record shows is narrower and more interesting. The banners and badges and the coffin did real work: they made the cost of an old browser visible, they gave big sites cover to set dates, and they gave Microsoft's own browser team a public reason to say what it plainly wanted to say. But the deceased had just under 20% of the market on the night of its wake, and it fell below 1% in the United States almost two years later, after its maker joined in. It outlived the funeral by four years of security patches.

What killed IE6 was never going to be persuasion, because the people being persuaded mostly weren't the ones deciding. It ended when the decision itself was designed out: browsers that update without asking, and a support policy that covers only the newest one. The lesson I'd take is to look for where an upgrade requires someone's permission, because that is where the next IE6 is already sitting. And if a competitor's joke about your product is fair, send flowers.

item.title: XMLHttpRequest: six years waiting for a name
item.description: Microsoft shipped the object behind every web application in 1999, under a name its author calls an excuse. Almost nobody used it until a designer's 2005 essay called the technique Ajax.
item.content:encoded:
The most important line of JavaScript of the 2000s shipped in 1999 with a name its own author calls an excuse, and then sat largely ignored for six years until somebody gave the technique around it a better one.

var req = new ActiveXObject(
  "Microsoft.XMLHTTP");

That is how you asked a server for something without leaving the page, in Internet Explorer 5, in March 1999. It isn't JavaScript's doing, strictly. ActiveXObject was Microsoft's way of letting script load a Windows component, the same door that opened Excel or the file system, and "Microsoft.XMLHTTP" was a component that happened to speak HTTP. The object it handed back could open a URL, send a request and give you the response as text. The page stayed where it was.

Every web application you use now is built on that ability. What I find worth an essay is the gap. The capability was in the dominant browser from 1999. The word "Ajax" arrived on February 18, 2005. In between, the object sat in the most widely used browser on earth and drew very little notice. The story of those six years is a story about a team with a deadline, a browser plug-in system, a recession and, in the end, a consultant who needed a shorter word for a client meeting.

Before: one click, one page

The web's original contract was simple. You clicked, the browser threw away the page, the server built a new one, and you waited. Jesse James Garrett, in the essay this story ends with, put the cost in one line: "While the server is doing its thing, what's the user doing? That's right, waiting."

Dynamic HTML, which arrived in 1997 and which split the web in two for a while, let a page change itself after it loaded. It did not let a page fetch anything new. Script could rearrange what the server had already sent, and that was all. If you wanted to check whether a username was taken, you submitted the form.

People found ways around this, and they were all smuggling operations. Anything with a src could carry a message to the server, so the standard trick was a frame the visitor couldn't see:

<iframe name="rpc" width="0" height="0"></iframe>

<script>
function checkName(name) {
  frames["rpc"].location =
    "check.asp?name=" + escape(name);
}
function gotResult(taken) {
  alert(taken ? "Taken" : "Available");
}
</script>

The server answered with a tiny HTML page whose only content was a script calling parent.gotResult(true). The response was, in effect, a function call sent as a web page. That is the Internet Explorer form; other browsers needed other hidden elements for the same trick. It failed in ways that were hard to see, because a hidden frame has no error handler and no status code you can read.

Microsoft had an official product in this space too. Brent Ashley's Remote Scripting page, which Ashley has kept online "for historical purposes", describes Microsoft Remote Scripting as solving the problem "by embedding a Java applet in the page to communicate with the server". A Java applet, to send a string. Ashley wrote a JavaScript-only alternative called JSRS "in the summer of 2000", built on hidden DHTML elements, and a second one called RSLite that passed its data in cookies. When people are carrying data in cookies on purpose, the platform is missing a feature.

A weekend in Redmond

The feature came from a mail team. Alex Hopmann, who worked on Exchange 2000 at Microsoft, wrote the history down in The Story of XMLHTTP, and it is the best primary source on any of this, so I'll lean on it.

Exchange needed a new Outlook Web Access, the webmail front end for corporate email. Hopmann dates the start to "probably sometime in late 1998". Two versions got underway: one of plain HTML pages, and one built with DHTML by Jim Van Eaton and Bob Gering. Of the first demo of the DHTML one, Hopmann writes, "I was just blown away". The DHTML one had a plumbing problem, though. In Hopmann's words, "they were basically doing hacky form-posts back to the server". So:

That weekend I startup up Visual Studio and whipped up the first version of what would become XMLHTTP. The first version didn't have async support hooked up and was pretty crude…

A component on one developer's machine doesn't help a product whose whole pitch is that you can walk up to any computer and read your mail. It had to be in the browser already. Internet Explorer 5 was, by Hopmann's account, "just weeks away from beta 2", its last beta. Another developer, Shawn Bracewell, rewrote the code to production quality and added the asynchronous mode and error handling. Hopmann, meanwhile, went looking for something that already shipped with Internet Explorer and could carry a stowaway. That turned out to be MSXML, Microsoft's XML parser library, whose team was run by Jean Paoli.

Which brings us to the name. I'd assumed for years that it was called XMLHTTP because it was designed to fetch XML. Hopmann says otherwise:

…the thing is mostly about HTTP and doesn't have any specific tie to XML other than that was the easiest excuse for shipping it so I needed to cram XML into the name (plus- XML was the hot technology at the time and it seemed like some good marketing for the component).

Two other lines from that account deserve to be better known. On security: "We did a quick security review but at the time no one really understood the seriousness or types of vulnerabilities that anything shipping could cause." And on quality: "no one other than OWA is going to try to call it so if it has a bug in the beta, worst case we just can't use it." The feature that would carry Gmail, Google Suggest and much of what got called Web 2.0 was checked in a week before a beta, on the theory that only one team would ever call it.

Internet Explorer 5 shipped in March 1999. Exchange 2000 and its Outlook Web Access followed, per Hopmann, "another year and a half" later. By then the piece it needed was on a great many desktops.

How the object worked

The API that went out in 1999 is, with small changes, the one in your browser today. A full request, as you'd have written it for Internet Explorer 5 or 6:

var req = new ActiveXObject("Microsoft.XMLHTTP");
req.onreadystatechange = function () {
  if (req.readyState == 4) {
    if (req.status == 200) {
      document.all["news"].innerHTML =
        req.responseText;
    }
  }
};
req.open("GET", "news.asp", true);
req.send(null);

Three things in there shaped a decade of code. The third argument to open is the async flag, and true meant your script carried on while the request was out. That one boolean is the A in Ajax. The callback fired on every state change, so everyone learned to test for the magic number 4; the W3C's first draft listed the states by name, and 4 was "Loaded". And the response came back two ways: as a string in responseText, or parsed into a document in responseXML if the server sent XML. Most people, most of the time, wanted the string.

Other browsers had no ActiveX, so they couldn't copy the component. They copied its interface instead and exposed it as a plain constructor, new XMLHttpRequest(), with Microsoft's method names and a spelling that capitalizes half an acronym. (Microsoft's own component was XMLHTTP, all capitals.) Wikipedia's history puts it in Mozilla's Gecko engine by 2002, in Safari 1.2 in 2004 and in Opera 8.0 in 2005. Aaron Swartz, looking back in A Brief History of Ajax, summed up those years: "Mozilla quickly followed suit and, while nobody I know used it, the function stayed there, just waiting to be taken advantage of."

Why it sat unused

Six years is a long time for a feature this useful to sit unused. I count four reasons, and I think they mattered in roughly this order.

It lived behind ActiveX. For the first few years the object existed in one browser on one operating system, behind the same mechanism that security-minded administrators were busy switching off. A public site that depended on it was betting on the visitor's browser and the visitor's IT department. Garrett, asked in a 2006 interview about the standards work then starting, said something that fits: people had tried to solve the problem "in proprietary ways for years", and the approach "didn't get traction until it was broadly available in a vendor-neutral way". The dates fit. Safari's support came in 2004, the year Gmail launched.

The timing was terrible. The object shipped in 1999 and the dot-com crash followed. Swartz's history has a bleak phrase for the period: "Shortly thereafter the bubble burst and web development crashed." The teams that might have spent 2001 building ambitious browser applications were mostly not employed to do so. Hopmann, explaining why the idea hadn't caught on even earlier, grants the slow connections and slow machines of the late 1990s ("typical machines were 200mhz") and then names what he thinks mattered most: developers don't make sweeping shifts quickly, and "these things take 3-5 years".

Nobody could see the examples. Outlook Web Access was the first big application built this way, and it lived behind corporate logins. Oddpost, a webmail service that opened in 2002 and behaved like a desktop mail client, charged a subscription, and Swartz reckons that is why it "didn't receive as much attention". Gmail launched on April 1, 2004, two and a half years after work on it began. Paul Buchheit recalls that along the way quite a few colleagues wanted it killed, or rebuilt with native client software, "not this crazy Javascript stuff". It was free, but its script was hard to follow. The breakthrough was the small one. Google Suggest appeared in December 2004, a search box that completed your query as you typed, and Hopmann notes that people "looked at the source code of that page to figure out how it worked". View Source was the school, and for once the lesson was short enough to read. Google Maps followed on February 8, 2005.

It had no name. Developers called it XMLHTTP, or remote scripting, or described it by pointing at Gmail. None of those fits on a slide. I think this reason is underrated, and the next section is my argument for it.

February 18, 2005

Ten days after Google Maps appeared, Jesse James Garrett of the San Francisco consultancy Adaptive Path published Ajax: A New Approach to Web Applications. Garrett was a user experience designer writing for other designers, and the essay reads that way. It has two diagrams and no code. The key sentences:

Google Suggest and Google Maps are two examples of a new approach to web applications that we at Adaptive Path have been calling Ajax. The name is shorthand for Asynchronous JavaScript + XML, and it represents a fundamental shift in what's possible on the Web.

Garrett was careful to say what the word covered: "Ajax isn't a technology. It's really several technologies", listed as XHTML and CSS, the DOM, XML and XSLT, XMLHttpRequest, and JavaScript "binding everything together". The essay claimed no invention. A follow-up Q&A three weeks later answered the obvious challenge directly: "Neither Adaptive Path nor Google invented Ajax." Asked why the thing needed a name at all, Garrett gave the most honest answer in the history of technical branding:

I needed something shorter than "Asynchronous JavaScript+CSS+DOM+XMLHttpRequest" to use when discussing this approach with clients.

In the 2006 interview Garrett filled in the scene. The technical people at a client already understood the pieces; the word was for "the business people I was dealing with". Then Garrett published the essay and "left the country", spending two weeks in Japan without internet access and coming home to "this avalanche of e-mail".

The speed of what followed is the evidence that the name was the missing part. On March 22, 2005, thirty-two days after the essay, Rails 0.11.0 shipped with the word in its release title and "Ajax helpers" as the headline feature. By the time Hopmann wrote his account, the term had reached the Wall Street Journal. Douglas Crockford, never one to oversell a trend, later described the moment this way: "In 2005, the idea of Dynamic HTML gained new energy and acceptance when it was renamed as Ajax."

Hopmann's verdict on his former employer is harsher than anything I'd write: "At Microsoft we totally blew the opportunity to evangelize and get out in front of this approach back in 1999."

Living with two constructors

Once everyone wanted to make requests, everyone needed the same few lines at the top of the file, because there were two ways to get the object. The canonical version is short enough that the Internet Explorer team published it themselves in January 2006:

if (window.XMLHttpRequest){
  // If IE7, Mozilla, Safari, etc: Use native object
  var xmlHttp = new XMLHttpRequest()
}
else
{
  if (window.ActiveXObject){
    // ...otherwise, use the ActiveX control for IE5.x and IE6
    var xmlHttp = new ActiveXObject("Microsoft.XMLHTTP");
  }
}

Read the first comment again. That post, by program manager Sunava Dutta, was announcing that Internet Explorer 7 would support "a scriptable native version of XMLHTTP", so that organizations which had disabled ActiveX could still run these applications. Microsoft was adopting the other browsers' imitation of Microsoft's own component, and putting itself on the "native object" branch of a test that had existed only to route around it. Internet Explorer 7 shipped in October 2006. The else branch stayed in libraries for years, since Internet Explorer 6 did too.

Careful versions of that snippet grew a ladder of try blocks, asking for "Msxml2.XMLHTTP" first and falling back to "Microsoft.XMLHTTP", because the component had been reissued under more than one name. Nobody wanted to write that twice, so the wrapper became the first thing every library offered. Prototype, the library that grew up alongside Rails, reduced a request to:

new Ajax.Request('/some_url', {
  method:'get',
  onSuccess: function(transport) {
    var response = transport.responseText || "no response text";
    alert("Success! \n\n" + response);
  },
  onFailure: function() { alert('Something went wrong...'); }
});

No readyState, no magic 4, no ActiveX. jQuery later did the same with $.ajax, and I'd guess a large share of working developers went a decade without typing XMLHttpRequest at all. The word in the method name was Garrett's.

The X went quietly. Garrett's own Q&A had already conceded that you didn't need XML, and could use "a technology like JavaScript Object Notation". Parsing a responseXML document with DOM calls was miserable next to getting an object you could use directly, and by December 2006 Crockford could tell an XML conference, to its face, that "JSON has become the X in Ajax".

What it left behind

A standard written by transcription. The W3C published its first working draft of "The XMLHttpRequest Object" on April 5, 2006, seven years after the object shipped. Its stated method was to "document a minimum set of interoperable features based on existing implementations", and it adds that "only features that are already implemented are considered". It also acknowledges being derived from the WHATWG's work documenting existing behavior. So the chain runs: a Microsoft team writes a component for its own product, other browsers reverse-engineer the interface, a group of browser people writes down what the copies do, and the standards body publishes that. I don't mean this as a complaint. It is how most of the platform you rely on got specified, and this is one of the cleanest examples.

A name nobody can fix. The current living standard carries a sentence I find oddly moving: "The name XMLHttpRequest is historical and has no bearing on its functionality." It was true the weekend the thing was written. The XML was a shipping excuse from the start, and the web will carry it for as long as there is a web, capital letters and all.

The synchronous flag outlived its reason. Hopmann's first version "didn't have async support hooked up", so the blocking mode came first and the famous one was added in the rewrite. A blocking request freezes the page while it waits, and browsers have been trying to remove it for years. The spec says synchronous requests outside of workers are "in the process of being removed from the web platform", and then adds, in brackets, "This is a long process that takes many years." A blocking mode from a weekend prototype is still being negotiated a quarter of a century later.

The engine in the diagram became the framework. Garrett's essay describes the browser loading "an Ajax engine", written in JavaScript, that is "responsible for both rendering the interface the user sees and communicating with the server on the user's behalf". In 2005 that was a box in a figure. It is also a fair description of what a single-page application framework does, written years before the big ones existed. The problems arrived with it. Garrett's Q&A lists, as open questions, accessibility, the back button, and what happens when JavaScript is off, and answers all of them with "maybe". The industry spent the next fifteen years turning those maybes into routers, history APIs and server rendering.

The security review came later. The rule browsers settled on was that a page could call only its own server, and the 2006 draft gives it one line: "Same-origin security restrictions SHOULD apply." Everything developers then wanted, calling other people's servers, needed a new permission system, which is where the 2008 Level 2 draft's "cross-site requests" and the CORS errors in your console come from. The "quick security review" of the late 1990s has been followed by a rather longer one.

The replacement, fetch, arrived in the mid-2010s, and MDN describes it as "a more powerful and flexible replacement for XMLHttpRequest". It returns a promise instead of counting to 4. The old constructor is still in every browser, and a great deal of code still calls it through one wrapper or another.

The takeaway

The capability and the name are different inventions, and the web needed both. Microsoft shipped the capability in 1999, for one product, under a name chosen to get it past a release deadline. It worked. Hardly anyone outside noticed, because it was locked to one browser, because the industry was in a slump, because the best examples were hidden behind logins and paywalls, and because nobody could say in a meeting what it was. Each of those took years to clear, and the last one was cleared in an afternoon's reading by a designer who had written no part of the code.

I'd argue that makes Garrett's essay a piece of engineering in its own right. Hopmann, who built the first version, came to the same view: "effective marketing and communication of your ideas is important and we missed out on that." A feature that can't be named can't be asked for, budgeted, taught or put in a job ad. The object had one name that was wrong from its first day and survived anyway; the technique had none for six years and stayed obscure until it got one.

  • Ajax: A New Approach to Web Applications, Jesse James Garrett, Adaptive Path, 2005 (a saved copy of the print view, with the March 2005 Q&A) (archived)
  • The story behind Ajax, interview with Jesse James Garrett by Brad Grimes and Joab Jackson, GCN, 2006
  • A Brief History of Ajax, Aaron Swartz, 2005 (archived)
